cards.text: Lamentations is a book of tears over Jerusalem after her people fell into the hands of the enemy (Lam 1:7). The poet just asked why any mortal man should complain, in view of his sins (Lam 3:39). Now he turns and speaks for everybody.

cards.question: After asking why anyone should complain in view of his sins, what does the poet call everyone to do?

answers.text: Examine our ways and turn back to the LORD
Rebuild the walls and wait for help to come
Leave the city and find a new home

cards.text: Examine and test our ways. Friend, that's me poking a batch to see if it's done. Except this time the batch is US. And he says to lift up our hearts and hands to God in heaven. Not just the hands. The whole baker.

cards.question: The prayer they lift up to God begins, “We have ___ and rebelled.”
In that same prayer, they tell God He has already forgiven them.

cards.text: No forgiveness yet. The words keep going, straight to God, and they get heavy: “You have covered Yourself in anger and pursued us; You have killed without pity.”

cards.question: The poet says God has covered Himself with a cloud. What can't pass through that cloud?

cards.text: A cloud no prayer can pass through. I bet that feels like calling somebody with ZERO bars. You keep talking. You keep checking the screen. Nothing.

cards.question: Among the nations around them, what does the poet say God has made them?
The poet goes on: “All our ___ open their mouths against us.”

cards.text: Panic and pitfall. Devastation and destruction. He's stacking the words two at a time. I think he can't find one word big enough.
Then it gets personal. It's not “us” anymore. He says, “Streams of tears flow from my eyes over the destruction of the daughter of my people.”

cards.question: The poet's eyes overflow without relief. How long does he say they'll keep overflowing?

answers.text: Until the LORD looks down and sees
Until the enemies leave the land
Until the city walls go back up

cards.question: The poet's eyes bring grief to his soul because of all the daughters of his city.

cards.text: Now the poet tells what his enemies did to him. Without cause, they hunted him like a bird. No reason. Just the chase.

cards.question: The enemies who hunted the poet caught him. Where did they drop him?

cards.text: Then they cast stones on him, and the waters flowed over his head. Friend, I spent years in the back of a junk drawer and thought THAT was the bottom. This man is in a pit. Under stones. Under WATER.

cards.question: With the water over his head in that pit, the poet thought he was going to die.
Out of the depths of the Pit, what does the poet do?

answers.text: He calls on the LORD's name
He goes quiet and gives up

cards.text: And the LORD heard him. The poet says, “You heard my plea: ‘Do not ignore my cry for relief.’”

cards.question: When the poet called from the Pit, the LORD drew near. What did the LORD say to him?

cards.text: Do not be afraid. Friend, I know a little something about lying in the dark and somebody showing up with words like that. It changes EVERYTHING.

cards.question: The poet tells the Lord, “You defend my ___, O Lord; You redeem my ___.”

cards.text: Then he lays it out. The LORD has seen the wrong done to him. All of it.

cards.question: Since the LORD has seen the wrong done to him, the poet asks the LORD to vindicate his cause.

cards.text: The LORD has seen all their malice and all their plots against him. He's heard their insults, and the slander and murmuring against the poet all day long.

cards.question: When his enemies sit and when they rise, they mock the poet in ___.

cards.text: Mocking him in song. Sitting down AND standing up. Friend, that's not a rough day. That's a group chat that NEVER goes quiet.

cards.question: The poet says the LORD will let his enemies go free.

cards.text: Nope. He says the LORD will pay them back what they deserve, according to the work of their hands. Then he asks the LORD to put a veil of anguish over their hearts: “may Your curse be upon them!”

cards.question: Back at the start, the poet said God had pursued us in anger. At the very end, who does he say the LORD will pursue in anger?

answers.text: The poet and his own people

findings.problem: The opening card uses two verses from outside the passage, Lam 1:7 and Lam 3:39, but its citation gives only Lamentations 3:39. Following the citation rule literally would give a range of Lamentations 1:7-3:39, which spans almost three chapters the card doesn't tell.
findings.question: How should a story card cite outside-passage context verses that aren't next to each other, like Lam 1:7 and Lam 3:39? Should it use one wide range, only the nearest verse, or something else?

findings.problem: The right answer, 'Examine our ways and turn back to the LORD', is almost the verse word for word and ends with 'the LORD'. The wrong answers are plain modern phrasing, so the right answer stands out as the Bible-sounding one.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.
